To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
all five cross-border migrants experienced cumulative agency constraints, felt vulnerable and were generally self-reliance but faced additional, citizenship-based exclusion.
the life stories of all five migrants are characterized by a lack of agency, a sense of vulnerability, and the need to rely on others to survive.

the life stories of the five cross-border migrants we interviewed revealed a range of vulnerabilities, including those related to structural violence, and that these vulnerabilities were exacerbated by the migrants’ exclusion from citizenship rights.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the implications of displacement, migration, structural violence and vulnerability for the practice of social work in South Africa.
conceptualising just responses to structural violence in urban areas, and the role of social work in this process.
the ways in which the subjectivities of cross-border migrants are constituted through their interactions with the state, civil society and other groups in South Africa.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the South African government should provide more services for the migrants and refugees, and the South African government and other countries should provide more services and opportunities to help migrants and refugees.
social workers should consider the implications of displacement, cross-border movement and structural violence for the lives of cross-border migrants.
social work needs to address both the structural violence of displacement and migration and the subjectivities of the people who are displaced and migrate.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
social work in South Africa needs to develop a more comprehensive understanding of the subjectivities of survival of those who are forced to move across borders, as well as those who remain.

the South African government should be encouraged to adopt an inclusive and rights-based approach to cross-border migration, and to provide services and support that are sensitive to migrants’ vulnerabilities and agency constraints.

we have to understand the subjectivities and experiences of people, especially in relation to the way in which they are positioned within a social structure and how they are able to negotiate this structure in order to achieve their aims.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the current social work response to cross-border migration in South Africa needs to be rethought.

the South African state’s failure to protect the rights of cross-border migrants and refugees has created a situation of structural vulnerability that is not only morally unjustifiable but also politically unsustainable.
social workers need to be able to conceptualise and address the subjectivities of survival in the context of displacement, cross-border mobility and structural violence.
